title: Why wet sand looks darker than dry sand
group: HOWN — How and Why in Nature
examples: Why does sand go dark when it gets wet?

explain.say: Dry sand is made of grains with air in between. Light bounces off grain after grain at every air gap and much of it soon comes back out to your eye, so dry sand looks pale.

faq.q: Why does sand go dark when it gets wet?
faq.a: Water fills the air gaps between grains. Light then scatters less and travels further into the sand, where more of it gets absorbed, so less light comes back and the sand looks darker.
asks: Why is wet sand a different colour?
Why is the sand dark near the sea?

faq.q: Why do wet clothes look darker?
faq.a: Fabric is full of tiny air gaps between fibres. Water fills them, so light scatters less and is absorbed more, and the wet patch looks darker than the dry cloth.
asks: Why does a wet T-shirt look darker?
Why does a spill leave a dark patch?

faq.q: Why does a wet road look darker?
faq.a: Water fills the rough gaps in the road surface, so light is absorbed more instead of being scattered back. Wet roads also act more like mirrors, reflecting headlights.
asks: Why are wet roads dark and shiny?
Why do roads change colour in rain?

faq.q: Why do wet things look more colourful?
faq.a: In dry sand, white light scattered from grain surfaces washes out the colour. When wet, there is less surface scattering and light travels deeper, picking up more of the grains' true colour.
asks: Why do wet pebbles look brighter?
Why are wet stones more colourful?

faq.q: Does wet sand turn light again when it dries?
faq.a: Yes. As the water evaporates, air fills the gaps again, light scatters back out, and the sand returns to its pale colour. Nothing about the grains has changed.
asks: Why does sand get lighter as it dries?
Is wet sand a different material?

facts: Wet sand, cloth and paper look darker because water filling the air gaps reduces scattering, so light travels further and more of it is absorbed.
Physicists John Lekner and Michael Dorf published an explanation of why wet things look darker in 1988.
